newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korean defector spent time in gulag --newspaper.
newsitem.headline: N.Korean defector spent time in gulag --newspaper.

text.p: A man claiming to be a North Korean has sought asylum in South Korea after arriving in Seoul's international airport on Sunday, and media reports said he was a former political prisoner.
Kang Chul-ho contacted South Korean authorities while in transit in Seoul on a flight from Beijing to Osaka, Japan, an intelligence official said on Monday.
Kang said he fled to China from North Korea in October 1992, said the official at the Agency for National Security Planning, who declined to be identified.
"We're still questioning him. We can't make any announcement at the moment," the official said.

The Chosun Ilbo newspaper said Kang's father was publicly executed in 1979 as an ideological foe of North Korea's Stalinist government, and that Kang was forced to denounce his father at the execution.
The newspaper, which based its report on an interview with Kang in China in 1994, said he spent three-and-a-half years in a political prison camp until 1991.

Last Thursday a North Korean woman in her 20s fled barefoot and hungry to South Korea through the heavily-mined and guarded Demilitarised Zone that has bisected the Korean peninsula since the end of the 1950-53 Korean War.

South Korea is negotiating with China for safe passage to Seoul of North Korea's top ideologue, who defected to a South Korean diplomatic mission in Beijing on February 12. However, the talks have so far been unsuccessful.
Near famine conditions in North Korea, and apparent disaffection among some members of the ruling elite, has prompted a string of defections in recent months.
Adding to an impression of instability, the country's defence minister and his deputy both died in quick succession last month, and the prime minister was replaced.
The domestic Yonhap news agency said Kang, 33, stepped off a Korean Air flight on Sunday and made a request for asylum to Seoul airport police in the transit lounge.

He was travelling under a fake name using forged Chinese seaman's papers and was on his way to Japan with 11 mainland Chinese and ethnic Korean Chinese seamen to work for a Japanese fishing company, Yonhap said.

"Because my father was executed publicly as an ideological offender and my mother and sister committed suicide, I was disillusioned with the North Korean system," Yonhap quoted Kang as telling investigators.
Kang had recently enrolled at a Chinese seamen's school after working as a labourer in the country, Yonhap said.

South Korean authorities have become wary of revealing personal details of North Korean asylum seekers since a high-profile defector, reportedly once related through marriage to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, was shot by two gunmen in a Seoul suburb on February 15.

Seoul police have said they believed North Korean hitmen were responsible and the assassination was intended as a warning to ideologue Hwang Jang-yop, now holed-up in Seoul's mission in Beijing, and other would-be defectors.
Nevertheless, the Chosun Ilbo published a picture of Kang at Seoul's Kimpo airport on Sunday.
Yonhap quoted an unnamed intelligence official as saying if Kang was confirmed to be a North Korean, South Korea would grant him asylum on humanitarian grounds.
South Korean officials believe there are hundreds, possibly thousands, of North Korean escapees in China and Russia waiting for the chance to flee to Seoul.
